title: Hanoi 2015: The City Conceded on Trees, Not on Accountability
content:
The Tree Hugs movement won the argument over trees and lost the argument over accountability. Its petition to Hanoi’s People’s Committee made three demands: stop the felling, open up the decision, and hold officials to account. The first was met within four days. The other two never were. That gap is the lesson.

The movement began with a dismissal. On 17 March 2015, a Hanoi propaganda official was asked whether residents had been consulted about plans to fell 6,700 street trees. There was no need, he replied. Within days, tens of thousands of Hanoians had answered him on Facebook.

No single organisation led the response. It was a loose network of three Facebook groups, drawing mostly young people and women.

The plan was approved in late 2013 without public notice. It would replace 6,708 trees on 190 streets for about US$3.4 million. Officials called it landscaping. Residents saw healthy, century old trees, many planted under French rule, falling within days in a city that shelters under their shade.

title: After School MeToo: Political Mamas’ Fight for Answers in South Korea
content: During South Korea’s 2018 School MeToo movement, students publicly reported sexual harassment and assault by teachers. But another question remained: how had schools and education authorities responded? In 2019, Political Mamas, a South Korean nonprofit founded by mothers, and open to other caregivers, began requesting records from regional education offices and mapping publicly reported allegations. The campaign aimed to make institutional responses visible, identify gaps in investigations and disciplinary action, and strengthen accountability for student safety.

title: Small Steps 4 Hannah: How One Family Helped Queensland See Coercive Control
content:
In February 2020, Hannah Clarke and her three children, Aaliyah, Laianah and Trey, were murdered in Brisbane, Queensland, Australia, by the husband she had recently left. Her father, Lloyd Clarke, kept asking how he had missed the signs.

Part of the answer was a term many people did not know yet: coercive control. It means using a pattern of behaviour to dominate a partner, such as cutting her off from family, tracking her, and controlling her money. This abuse often leaves no visible injuries.

Within weeks, Hannah’s parents, Sue and Lloyd Clarke, set up the Small Steps 4 Hannah Foundation. It supports people affected by domestic violence, teaches students, workers and families to spot coercive control, and has pushed the Queensland Government to make it a crime. This post argues that Small Steps used one family’s story to make hidden abuse visible and help write it into law in 2024. Whether the law brings real safety is still unclear.

title: The Right to Sit: How Kerala’s Women Retail Workers Pushed for Change
content:
The Right to Sit campaign in Kerala organized women textile workers around a simple demand—seating at work—and turned their shared grievances into a 2018 legal amendment mandating seats in shops and commercial establishments. The following article discusses their campaign and the need for workers to keep organizing and monitoring conditions to defend protections.

For many women working in Kerala’s textile shops in India, sitting down was something they had to fight for. They spent long hours on their feet, and some were not even allowed to lean against a wall. Workers reported knee pain and restrictions on toilet breaks. Some avoided drinking water because their shops lacked toilet facilities.

title: Voters repudiated Trump. Grassroots momentum will shape what comes next.
content:
This article was originally published on Waging Nonviolence and Truthout.

The broad strokes of the midterms are clear: a massive repudiation of MAGA’s fascist wave has ended the Trump 2.0 era of congressional complicity with his authoritarian takeover. Trump’s lame duck presidency now begins. 

This lopsided electoral rejection is historically rare: Flipping control of both the House and Senate in a midterm has only occurred three times since World War II (1946, 1994 and 2006). The breakthroughs are astounding: the first Native American female governor and senator, five Black governors, the first majority of Democratic governors in 16 years, and critical downballot wins like the first Democrat to win as Texan oil regulator since 1990 and the first openly transgender state legislator in Alabama.

title: First Nations Resources: Start Here
content:
Welcome to the First Nations Resources topic in the Commons Social Change Library. This article guides you through a wide range of materials designed to inform and educate people engaged in social change on topics important to First Nations people. Many of the resources in this topic are particularly for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander campaigners. These and other resources will also be beneficial to people acting in solidarity.

Although this First Nations topic mostly has an Australian focus, we would like to acknowledge the importance of Indigenous struggles for sovereignty, self-determination and justice all around the world. International struggles for First Nations justice often reflect, support, and inform First Nations movements and issues here in Australia and elsewhere in the colonised world. 

To help navigate this topic, we’ve outlined examples from four broad types of resources:

  • resources describing First Nations campaign stories both within Australia and internationally;
  • resources that amplify First Nations voices and perspectives;
  • resources for First Nations people engaged in social change;

title: Justice, Diversity & Inclusion: Start Here
content:
Welcome to the Justice, Diversity and Inclusion topic in the Commons Social Change Library. We believe that strong movements are made up of diverse participants, each bringing their particular talents, perspectives, and community connections. Developing such movements requires an appreciation for the value of diversity, as well as experience including, and working in solidarity with, those who are marginalised by the dominant assumed common culture. The restructuring of power relations and real engagement with justice concerns are necessary for true inclusion.

To help navigate within the broad scope this topic includes, we’ve outlined examples from four types of resources:

  • resources that clarify key concepts used in movements seeking to improve diversity and inclusion practices;
  • resources to help those building capacity to recognise and resist oppression of all forms, such as by seeking out diverse perspectives and recognising and leveraging privileges.
  • advice for taking action, including specific acts of inclusion, acts of solidarity, and acts of resistance.

title: Workers Rights Hub: Start Here
content:
This collection is developed in partnership with IRIS, the International Resource for Impact and Storytelling, as part of the Future of Work(ers) project.

Start here by exploring their collection. Fill in this form if you would like to submit a resource.

When Flight Attendants fought the Airline Industry and Won
Watch this Vox video on the “stewardess rebellion,” where flight attendants fought and overturned discriminatory, sexualised airline practices, transforming their profession and advancing women’s workplace rights.

Gig Workers, Organising, Unions and Algorithms: A Curated Collection
This collection brings together key research, guides, case studies and analyses exploring how gig workers navigate digital platforms, work instability, unions and algorithms.

Exploring the Gig Economy: Challenges and Opportunities Toolkit
This toolkit is a practical resource to better understand the online gig economy, whether for personal learning or to support awareness-raising and training sessions. It is a learning guide with detailed explanations, real-life examples and insights into online gig work.

title: Working in Groups: Start Here
content:
Welcome to the Working in Groups topic in the Commons Social Change Library. Effective and lasting change tends to be the result of people working together in groups and networks towards a shared goal. Social change can’t be won by isolated individuals, it requires us to do the rewarding but sometimes messy work of collaborating with others.

This topic is designed to offer a range of resources to help organisations and individuals be more informed, intentional and skilled when engaging in group work.

For groups to work effectively there needs to be a level of coordination, collaboration, promotion of diversity, and the skills to participate and facilitate well. Conflict and power dynamics are inherent parts of group life that can be understood, prepared for and responded to. Team work and morale can be fostered and built.

You can search within the topic by using the ‘Refine by Format’, ‘Refine by Author’, and ‘Refine by Collection’ filter functions. The ‘Refine by Topic’ option will assist in applying a filter that will identify resources which cross over with other topics within the Commons Social Change Library (e.g. Diversity & Inclusion).

title: Communications and Media: Start Here
content:
Creating change requires engaging audiences, communicating messages, and inviting people to join in action. The resources here will help you get clearer on what communication channels to use and how, how to develop compelling framing and messages, and the skills required to engage media (traditional and new forms) effectively.

This guide will help you navigate the Communications and Media topic on the Commons Library. You may also like to check out our Story and Narrative topic, Digital Campaigning topic and Countering Disinformation project collection.
